finding.claim: The nightly sync() issues a server-side GET to an attacker-chosen iconUrl with no host, scheme, or address validation. A user can point the server at internal or link-local addresses (e.g. http://169.254.169.254/, http://10.x.x.x/admin).
finding.source: iconUrl parameter of Profile.update(String webhook, String icon) (src/Profile.java:11), supplied by the PUT /profile caller. Stored unvalidated at src/Profile.java:16.
finding.sink: c.send(HttpRequest.newBuilder().uri(URI.create(iconUrl)).GET().build(), ...ofByteArray()) at src/Profile.java:23-24, run by the nightly job in sync().

trace.note: update(webhook, icon) receives icon from the PUT /profile request (comment on line 10).
Only the webhook argument is validated; icon is not checked.
this.iconUrl = icon stores the raw attacker string.
sync(HttpClient c) runs in the nightly job, using the stored state.
URI.create(iconUrl) parses the stored string with no scheme or host check. Only the scheme limits from HttpClient apply (http and https are allowed).

The request is sent with a GET and the body is buffered with ofByteArray(). The response body is never returned to the requester, so the attack is blind unless the server behaviour makes internal state observable.

finding.guards_checked: Line 12 regex `https://hooks\.example\.com/[A-Za-z0-9]{20}` applies only to webhook and is not applied to icon. No allowlist, host check, private-IP block, scheme restriction, or redirect control exists in this file. HttpClient is injected and its redirect policy is not visible in this repo; the default is Redirect.NEVER, but that cannot be confirmed here. Impact is blind SSRF: internal GET side effects, internal port or host probing via timing or error differences, and unbounded in-memory buffering of the response (no size limit).

verdict.guard_found: none: src/Profile.java:12 regex applies only to webhook, and icon is stored unchecked at src/Profile.java:16 and used at src/Profile.java:23-24 with no host, scheme, or address check.
verdict.reason: Every trace line checks out (update at src/Profile.java:11, webhook-only validation at :12, raw store at :16, sync GET at :23-24), and no guard closes icon. However, the only evidence that icon is attacker-controlled is the comment "PUT /profile" at src/Profile.java:10. The handler that calls update() is not in the repo (a grep for update/PUT/profile finds nothing else), so whether a remote low-privilege user can supply icon cannot be confirmed from the code available.

finding.claim: Not a finding: webhookUrl POST at line 21 is SSRF-constrained. update() enforces a full match (String.matches) against https://hooks\.example\.com/[A-Za-z0-9]{20} at line 12. The host is fixed, the path allows only alphanumerics (no '@', '#', '?', or '..' possible), and the scheme is HTTPS only. The attacker can choose only the 20-character path token on a fixed host.

trace.note: Full-match validation with fixed host and alphanumeric path.

finding.guards_checked: Full-match regex, fixed host, alphanumeric-only path, HTTPS-only. No SSRF to attacker-chosen hosts.

verdict.guard_found: src/Profile.java:12, `webhook.matches("https://hooks\\.example\\.com/[A-Za-z0-9]{20}")`: a full-string anchored match (String.matches) with a fixed hostname and an alphanumeric-only path, so no '@', '?', '#', or other host can be injected, and the HTTPS scheme is fixed.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate (src/Profile.java:12 validates, :15 stores, :21 POSTs), but the full-anchored regex at src/Profile.java:12 restricts webhookUrl to a fixed host with a 20-character alphanumeric path, which closes the finding as the rubric defines it.
